page.title: Command Centre
page.description: Your AI workforce at a glance — schedules, live tasks, and agent reports.

working_now.text: Agents actively processing tasks right now.

channels_live.text: Active communication channels (Slack, email, etc.) currently connected.

completed_today.text: Total tasks finished by all agents in the last 24 hours.

needs_attention.text: Items that need your review — failed tasks, low-quality reports, or expiring connections.

schedule.text: Upcoming automated routines. Created through Recipes with cron triggers. Click any item to view or edit.

active_now.text: Tasks currently in progress with real-time progress bars. Shows agent, step count, and elapsed time.

view_report.text: Open the full report submitted by this agent. Reports include findings, actions taken, and referenced files.

grade.text: Rate this report's quality (1-5 stars). Grading helps track agent performance over time.

search.text: Search across all stored agent memories using natural language. Uses vector similarity for semantic matching.

delete.text: Permanently remove this memory. The agent will no longer recall this information.

page.title: Agent Management
page.description: Create, configure, and monitor your AI workforce.

total_agents.text: Total agents in your workspace. Each agent is a specialised AI worker with its own model, skills, and tools.

active_agents.text: Agents currently online and ready to process tasks. Idle agents are configured but not actively running.

categories.text: Distinct agent types in your workspace (code_architect, security_expert, custom, etc.).

avg_performance.text: Average success rate across all agents. Target: >90%. Based on task completion without errors.

search.text: Filter agents by name, type, or capabilities. Results update in real-time as you type.

status_filter.text: Toggle between Active (online, processing) and Idle (configured but not running) agents.

create_button.text: Create a new agent. Choose from templates (Code Reviewer, Sentinel, etc.) or start from scratch.

template_selection.text: Templates come pre-configured with a system prompt, recommended model, and skills. You can customise everything after creation.

name.text: A descriptive name helps the router match messages to this agent. Be specific: 'JavaScript Code Reviewer' beats 'Reviewer'.

description.text: The Universal Router uses this description to decide when to send messages to this agent. Be clear about what it handles.

model_selection.text: The LLM that powers this agent. Different models have different strengths, speeds, and costs.

temperature.text: Controls creativity. 0 = deterministic and focused. 1 = creative and varied. Most agents work well at 0.7.

max_tokens.text: Maximum response length. Higher = longer responses but more expensive. 2000-3000 works for most tasks.

skills.text: Skills give agents domain expertise. They enhance the system prompt with specialised knowledge. 3-7 skills per agent is typical.

tools.text: External app integrations (GitHub, Slack, Jira). Only assigned tools can be used by this agent.

success_rate.text: Percentage of tasks completed without errors over the last 30 days.

tasks_completed.text: Total number of tasks this agent has handled since creation.

temperature.text: Controls how random or creative the agent's responses are. 0 = always picks the most likely word (deterministic, good for code and data). 1+ = more varied and creative (good for writing and brainstorming). Most agents work well at 0.5-0.7.
temperature.example: Code review → 0.2 | Marketing copy → 0.9 | General assistant → 0.7

max_tokens.text: The maximum number of tokens (roughly words) the agent can generate in a single response. Higher values allow longer answers but cost more. 1 token ≈ 0.75 words.
max_tokens.example: Quick answers → 500 | Detailed reports → 3000 | Code generation → 4000

top_p.text: Nucleus sampling — limits the model to choosing from the top P% most likely tokens. Lower values make output more focused. Usually leave at 1.0 unless you need very constrained output. Adjusting both temperature and Top P at once can produce unpredictable results.
top_p.example: 0.1 = very narrow (only top 10% of tokens) | 1.0 = full vocabulary

frequency_penalty.text: Penalises tokens that have already appeared in the response, reducing word-for-word repetition. Higher values make the agent avoid repeating the same phrases. 0 = no penalty, 2 = strong penalty.
frequency_penalty.example: 0.0 = allow repetition | 0.5 = mild variety | 1.5 = strongly avoid repeating words

presence_penalty.text: Encourages the agent to talk about new topics rather than staying on the same subject. Unlike frequency penalty, this applies equally whether a token appeared once or many times. Higher values push for more diverse content.
presence_penalty.example: 0.0 = stay focused | 0.6 = balanced | 1.5 = explore many topics

fallback_model.text: A backup model that kicks in if the primary model is unavailable, rate-limited, or returns an error. Useful for reliability — pick a cheaper, faster model as fallback.

enable.text: Heartbeats let your agent wake up on a schedule and autonomously check its environment — monitor inboxes, review dashboards, scan for changes. Think of it as a cron job for your AI agent.

interval.text: How often the agent wakes up and runs its heartbeat task. Shorter intervals catch issues faster but use more tokens. Start with hourly and adjust based on need.
interval.example: Monitoring bot → 15 min | Daily digest → 1440 min (daily)

active_hours.text: Restrict heartbeats to specific hours. Useful to avoid unnecessary runs overnight. 'Inherit from orchestrator' uses your workspace's global active hours setting.

prompt.text: Instructions the agent follows during each heartbeat. Be specific about what to check, what actions to take, and what to report back. This is the agent's autonomous task definition.
prompt.example: Check the GitHub repo for new PRs, summarise changes, and flag any security concerns.

auto_act.text: When enabled, the agent can take action based on what it finds (e.g., send a Slack message, create an issue). When disabled, it only observes and reports — safer for new setups.

report_to.text: Where heartbeat results are delivered. 'Orchestrator' stores in the database (visible in Activity → Reports). 'Direct' shows in chat. Channel options send to your connected integrations.

edit_button.text: Modify this agent's model, prompt, persona, or tool assignments. Changes take effect immediately.

delegation.text: Controls whether this agent can pass tasks to other agents. Auto-delegate is faster but less controlled.

strategy.text: How agents work together on a task. Sequential = one at a time in order. Parallel = all work simultaneously. Hierarchical = lead agent delegates. Mesh = all communicate freely. Adaptive = switches strategy based on the task.
strategy.example: Code review → Sequential (reviewer then approver) | Research → Parallel (multiple experts) | Complex project → Hierarchical (PM delegates)

reasoning.text: How the group reaches a final answer when multiple agents contribute. Majority Vote = most common answer wins. Weighted Consensus = agents with higher success rates have more influence. Expert Selection = picks the best single response.

create.text: Create a multi-step workflow that chains multiple agents together. Define steps, inputs, and schedule.

schedule.text: Set a cron schedule to run this recipe automatically. E.g., daily at 23:00 for nightly reviews.

input.text: Type your message and press Enter. The Universal Router automatically sends it to the best agent.

auto_mode.text: Auto mode routes messages to the best agent automatically using cache, rules, semantic matching, and LLM classification.

agent_selector.text: Override auto-routing by selecting a specific agent. Your message goes directly to that agent.

code.text: Start a coding task. Routes to code-focused agents like Code Reviewer or QA Engineer.

create_agent.text: Launch the agent creation flow without leaving chat.

knowledge_base.text: Ask questions about your uploaded documents. Uses RAG to find relevant answers.

recipes.text: Browse and trigger multi-step workflows that coordinate multiple agents.

edit_tools.text: Quick access to manage tool assignments for your agents.

page.title: Tools & Integrations
page.description: Connect external apps and assign them to agents.

connected.text: Apps currently authenticated and available for agent use.

available.text: Total integrations available through Composio. 500+ apps across all categories.

developer.text: GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Linear — code repos, issues, PRs, and project management.

communication.text: Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord — messaging, channels, and notifications.

crm.text: Salesforce, HubSpot, Pipedrive — customer data and sales workflows.

permissions.text: Control what this agent can do. Full access = read and write. Read only = fetch data but not modify. Start with read-only for new agents.

credential.text: Which API credential to use for authentication. Configure credentials in Settings first.

connection_health.text: Shows whether the OAuth token or API key is valid. Expired connections need re-authentication.

page.title: Knowledge Bases
page.description: Documents, databases, and code repositories your agents can search.

total_documents.text: Total files uploaded and processed in your knowledge base.

processed.text: Files fully chunked, embedded, and searchable. Processing includes text extraction, semantic chunking, and vector embedding.

storage_used.text: Total storage consumed in S3 for your workspace's documents.

vector_chunks.text: Number of searchable embedding chunks. Each document is split into multiple chunks for precise retrieval.

search.text: Search documents by filename, content, or tags. Filters the library in real-time.

semantic_mode.text: Finds conceptually similar content even with different words. Uses AI embeddings for understanding-based search.

similarity_score.text: How relevant this result is to your query. 90-100% = excellent, 70-89% = good, below 50% = weak match.

drag_drop.text: Drag files here or click to browse. Supports PDF, DOCX, MD, TXT, code files, CSV, and JSON.

extraction.text: Extracting text from the file format. Also handles tables, images (OCR), and embedded content.

chunking.text: Splitting into semantic segments for search. Uses content boundaries, not arbitrary character counts.

embedding.text: Converting text chunks into vector embeddings for semantic search. Uses the configured embedding model.

indexing.text: Storing embeddings in the vector database. Once indexed, the content is searchable by all agents.

status.text: Shows how many files have been downloaded, processed, and indexed from your cloud folder.

sync_button.text: Trigger an incremental sync — only new or modified files are downloaded and processed.

retrieval_strategy.text: How documents are searched. Similarity = pure vector search (fast, semantic). BM25 = keyword matching (good for exact terms). Hybrid = combines both for best accuracy at slight speed cost.
retrieval_strategy.example: General Q&A → Similarity | Legal/medical terms → BM25 | Production → Hybrid

top_k.text: Maximum number of document chunks returned per query. More chunks = more context but slower and more expensive. 3-5 is typical for focused answers, 10+ for research tasks.

similarity_threshold.text: Minimum similarity score (0-1) for a chunk to be included in results. Higher = only very relevant matches. Lower = more results but some may be weak matches.
similarity_threshold.example: 0.8 = strict (fewer, highly relevant) | 0.5 = loose (more results, some noise)

hybrid_weight.text: Balance between vector search and keyword search in hybrid mode. 0.7 = 70% vector + 30% keyword. Higher vector weight favours semantic meaning; higher keyword weight favours exact term matching.

graph_hops.text: In knowledge graph retrieval, how many relationship levels to traverse from the initial match. 1 hop = direct connections only. 2+ hops = follows chains of relationships (broader but slower).

projects_indexed.text: Code repositories indexed as a knowledge graph. Agents can search code semantically.

relationships.text: Code relationships mapped — imports, function calls, class inheritance. Enables dependency and impact analysis.

page.title: Community Marketplace
page.description: Discover and install agents, recipes, tools, LLMs, and capability packages.

total_items.text: All items available across all marketplace tabs.

featured.text: Curated and highlighted items recommended for your workspace.

total_installs.text: Items you've installed into your workspace. Installed items are copies — safe to customise.

tool_count.text: Number of actions this app provides. E.g., GitHub has 50+ actions (create issue, review PR, search code).

added.text: This app is already connected to your workspace. Go to Tools to manage it.

install.text: Install this agent into your workspace. It comes pre-configured with a tuned prompt, model recommendation, and skill set.

pricing.text: Cost per million tokens (input/output). Actual costs depend on usage — track them in Analytics → LLM & Costs.

context_window.text: Maximum token capacity for a single request. Larger windows handle more context but cost more.

plugins.text: Bundled packages containing skills, commands, and agent configurations. Install once to get everything.

skills.text: Individual capability modules loaded from git repositories. Give agents specific domain expertise.

page.title: Team Management
page.description: Manage workspace members and access control.

invite.text: Send an email invitation to join this workspace. They'll sign in via Clerk and get a fresh workspace context.

role.text: Admin = full access including settings and team management. Member = create and use agents. Viewer = read-only.

remove.text: Revoke this person's access to the workspace. Their data (chat history, reports) is retained.

page.title: Analytics
page.description: Performance metrics, cost tracking, and optimisation insights.

success_rate.text: Percentage of tasks completed without errors. Target: >90%. Green = >90%, Yellow = 80-90%, Red = <80%.

total_executions.text: Total agent tasks completed in the selected time period.

avg_response_time.text: Mean time from request to response across all agents.

utilization.text: How busy are your agents? 60-80% is optimal. Below 40% = underutilised, above 90% = overloaded.

total_cost.text: Total LLM spend for the selected period across all providers and models.

total_tokens.text: Input + output tokens consumed. Input tokens are your prompts, output tokens are model responses.

cost_per_request.text: Average cost per API call. Varies by model — check the By Model breakdown to optimise.

top_spender.text: The agent or model consuming the most budget. Investigate if one agent dominates costs.

cost_projection.text: Projected monthly cost based on recent usage patterns. Estimate only — actual costs depend on usage changes.

error_rate.text: Percentage of failed tool calls. High rates usually mean an expired connection or rate limiting.

page.title: Settings
page.description: System configuration, credentials, and audit logs.

name.text: A label to identify this credential. E.g., 'Production OpenRouter', 'Dev Composio Key'.

test_connection.text: Verify the key is valid before saving. Catches typos and expired keys early.

types.text: Pre-configured credential schemas for each provider. Select the type, then paste your key.

audit.text: Every credential access is logged. View who used what and when in the audit trail.

default_model.text: The fallback model used when an agent doesn't specify one. OpenRouter gives access to 100+ models through one key.

embedding_model.text: Model used for document chunking and semantic search. Changing this requires re-processing all documents.

workspace_name.text: Display name for your workspace, shown to all team members.

feature_flags.text: Toggle platform features on or off. E.g., agent memory, cloud sync, workspace execution.

provider.text: LLM provider for the orchestrator (separate from agent models). Used for routing and task decomposition.

temperature.text: Orchestrator creativity. Lower = more consistent routing. Recommended: 0.3.

api_limit.text: Maximum API calls per minute across all users. Protects against overload. Default: 1,000 req/min.

provider.text: The AI company whose models power your orchestrator. OpenRouter recommended — gives access to 100+ models from all providers through a single API key.

model.text: The specific AI model the orchestrator uses for routing, task decomposition, and chat. Larger models reason better but cost more and respond slower.

thinking_level.text: Controls how much 'thinking time' the model gets before responding. Higher levels produce better reasoning but use more tokens. Off = instant responses, High = deep analysis with chain-of-thought.
thinking_level.example: Quick chat → Off or Minimal | Complex tasks → Medium or High

temperature.text: Controls randomness in the orchestrator's responses. 0 = always picks the most likely answer (best for routing). Higher values add variety. This is separate from individual agent temperatures.

max_tokens.text: Maximum length of the orchestrator's response. The orchestrator mainly routes and summarises, so 2000-4000 is usually enough. Higher values cost more per request.

timeout.text: How long to wait for the LLM to respond before giving up. Increase for complex queries or slow providers. Too low = frequent timeouts; too high = users wait unnecessarily.

retry_attempts.text: How many times to retry a failed LLM call before returning an error. Handles transient network issues and rate limits. 3 retries is a good default.

concurrent_requests.text: Maximum parallel API calls to the LLM provider. Higher = faster multi-agent workflows but risks hitting rate limits. Start low and increase if you see bottlenecks.

cache_ttl.text: How long (in seconds) to cache identical LLM responses. Saves money on repeated queries. 0 = no caching. 300 (5 min) is a good default. Set higher for stable content.

top_p.text: Nucleus sampling for the orchestrator. Limits token selection to the top P% most likely tokens. Usually leave at 1.0 unless you need very constrained routing decisions.

frequency_penalty.text: Reduces word-for-word repetition in orchestrator responses. 0 = no penalty. Higher values force more varied phrasing. Usually 0 is fine for the orchestrator.

presence_penalty.text: Encourages the orchestrator to cover new topics. 0 = stay focused on the task. Higher values push for broader responses. Usually 0 for routing tasks.

stop_sequences.text: Tokens that tell the model to stop generating. Comma-separated. Useful for structured output formats. Most users don't need to change this.
stop_sequences.example: \n\n = stop at double newline | ### = stop at section break

personality_mode.text: Pre-built personality templates that shape how the AI communicates. Friendly = casual and warm. Professional = formal and precise. Technical = detailed and code-focused. Custom = write your own.

custom_soul.text: Free-form instructions that define the AI's personality, tone, and behaviour. This is injected into every orchestrator call as a system prompt. Keep it concise — each token costs money on every request.

communication_style.text: Controls response length. Concise = short, direct answers. Balanced = moderate detail. Detailed = thorough explanations with examples. Affects all orchestrator responses.

proactive_level.text: What the AI does when its heartbeat discovers something. Silent = just logs it. Notify = alerts you. Act & Notify = takes action and tells you. Autonomous = acts without asking.
proactive_level.example: New users → Notify | Trusted setup → Act & Notify | Full auto → Autonomous

enable.text: The orchestrator heartbeat is a global check-in that monitors your entire workspace — agent health, pending tasks, channel status. Individual agent heartbeats are separate.

interval.text: How often the orchestrator runs its health check. Shorter = more responsive but uses more tokens. Daily is fine for most setups; hourly for production workloads.

active_hours.text: Restrict heartbeats to business hours to save tokens. The orchestrator won't wake up outside these hours. Times are in your local timezone.

checklist.text: A multi-line checklist of things the orchestrator should check during each heartbeat. One item per line. Be specific about what to monitor and what action to take.
checklist.example: Check all agent heartbeat statuses\nReview failed tasks from last hour\nVerify Slack connection is healthy

notification_channel.text: Where heartbeat results are sent. In-app = visible in Activity dashboard. Telegram/Slack = push to your connected channel. Useful for monitoring outside the platform.

provider.text: Service that converts text into vector embeddings for semantic search. OpenRouter recommended — access to 20+ models through one API key with parallel batch processing.
provider.example: OpenRouter (best value) | OpenAI (direct) | HuggingFace Local (free, slow)

model.text: The specific model used to create embeddings. Higher dimensions = more nuanced understanding but more storage. Changing this requires re-processing ALL documents.
model.example: Qwen3 8B (4096d, $0.01/M) — best value | Gemini (3072d) — top quality

vector_dimensions.text: Number of dimensions in each embedding vector. Auto-set based on your model choice. Higher dimensions capture more meaning but use more storage and compute.

vector_store_type.text: Where vector embeddings are stored and searched. PgVector uses your existing PostgreSQL database. Other options require separate infrastructure.
vector_store_type.example: PgVector (recommended, no extra setup) | Pinecone (managed, scalable) | FAISS (in-memory, fast)

max_seq_length.text: Maximum number of tokens the embedding model processes per chunk. Longer sequences capture more context per chunk but take longer to process. Must match your model's limit.

chunk_size.text: How many tokens each document chunk contains. Smaller chunks = more precise search results but more storage. Larger chunks = more context per result but less precision.
chunk_size.example: 256 = precise, many chunks | 512 = balanced | 1000+ = broad context

chunk_overlap.text: How many tokens overlap between adjacent chunks. Prevents important information from being split across chunk boundaries. 10-20% of chunk size is typical.

max_context_length.text: Maximum total tokens injected into the LLM prompt from retrieved documents. Higher = more context for the agent but costs more tokens per request.
max_context_length.example: 2000 = concise answers | 4000 = detailed context | 8000 = max depth

enable.text: Reranking uses a cross-encoder model to re-score search results after vector search. Improves retrieval precision by 15-30% at ~$0.002 per query. Requires a Cohere API key.

model.text: Which Cohere reranking model to use. rerank-v3.5 is the latest and highest quality. Multilingual version works across languages.

environment.text: Controls logging verbosity, error display, and debug features. Development = verbose logging + debug tools. Staging = moderate. Production = minimal logging, no debug.

log_level.text: Minimum severity level for log output. DEBUG = everything (verbose). INFO = normal operations. WARNING = potential issues. ERROR = failures only. CRITICAL = system-breaking only.

store_max_chars.text: How many characters of each message (user + assistant) are sent to Mem0 for fact extraction. Higher values preserve richer conversation context for recall but use more OpenAI tokens per save.
store_max_chars.example: 1500 = headlines only | 6000 = full conversations (~1500 words) | 12000 = detailed technical discussions

daily_log_max_chars.text: Max size for daily activity log summaries that agents reference for recent context. These are appended to prompts, so larger = better recall but more tokens per request.
daily_log_max_chars.example: 2000 = concise daily notes | 5000 = detailed activity log

context_budget_total.text: Total token budget for ALL memory injected into agent prompts. Split across session, long-term, temporal, and daily layers. Higher = better recall but every request costs more.

context_budget_session.text: Tokens reserved for L1 session memory — the rolling summary of the current conversation. Higher values help agents track longer multi-turn conversations.
context_budget_session.example: 300 = short chats | 500 = normal | 1000 = complex multi-step sessions

context_budget_long_term.text: Tokens reserved for L3 long-term Mem0 memories — facts extracted from past conversations. This is what lets agents 'remember' you said something last week.
context_budget_long_term.example: 500 = a few facts | 800 = good recall | 1500 = extensive history

context_budget_temporal.text: Tokens reserved for L2 short-term/temporal memories — recent exchanges stored in Postgres. Bridges the gap between session and long-term memory.
context_budget_temporal.example: 400 = recent highlights | 600 = balanced | 1000 = full recent context

context_budget_daily.text: Tokens reserved for daily activity logs — summaries of what happened each day. Helps agents know 'we did X yesterday' without loading the full conversation history.
context_budget_daily.example: 200 = just headlines | 400 = good overview | 800 = detailed daily log

search_result_limit.text: Maximum number of memories returned per search query. More results = broader recall but adds to prompt size. Mem0 ranks by relevance, so the top N are usually the best.
search_result_limit.example: 5 = focused recall | 8 = balanced | 15 = cast a wide net

long_term_search_limit.text: How many Mem0 long-term memories are fetched and injected into agent prompts. These are the 'remember when we discussed...' facts. More = richer context, more tokens.
long_term_search_limit.example: 3 = just the essentials | 5 = good balance | 10 = deep history injection

circuit_breaker_threshold.text: How many consecutive Mem0 failures trigger the circuit breaker. When open, all memory calls are fast-rejected instead of timing out — protecting agent response times.
circuit_breaker_threshold.example: 3 = aggressive protection | 5 = balanced | 10 = tolerant of flaky connections

circuit_breaker_cooldown.text: How long (seconds) the circuit breaker stays open before attempting Mem0 again. During cooldown, memory saves silently skip. Too short = hammers a broken service; too long = slow recovery.

request_timeout.text: Timeout for individual Mem0 API calls. Mem0 calls OpenAI internally for fact extraction, so it can be slow. Too low = frequent timeouts; too high = blocks agent responses.

cache_ttl.text: How long Mem0 search results are cached in Redis. Avoids repeated identical queries within the window. Lower = fresher results but more Mem0 API calls.
cache_ttl.example: 60s = near-realtime | 300s = balanced (5 min) | 900s = aggressive caching (15 min)

session_ttl.text: How long L1 session memory (current conversation context) lives in Redis before expiring. After expiry, a new conversation starts fresh without session history.

decay_rate.text: How fast memories lose importance over time. Higher decay = faster forgetting. Memories below the archive threshold get cleaned up. This controls the 'forgetting curve'.
decay_rate.example: 0.05 = slow fade (remembers longer) | 0.1 = balanced | 0.25 = aggressive pruning

promotion_min_importance.text: Minimum importance score for a L2 (short-term) memory to be promoted to L3 (long-term Mem0). Higher = only the most important facts persist permanently.
promotion_min_importance.example: 0.5 = promote liberally | 0.7 = balanced | 0.9 = only critical facts

promotion_min_access_count.text: How many times a memory must be accessed (retrieved in searches) before it qualifies for L3 promotion. Ensures only frequently-referenced memories become permanent.
promotion_min_access_count.example: 1 = promote on first recall | 3 = balanced | 5 = must prove its worth

type.text: How this recipe gets triggered. Manual = click to run. Scheduled = runs on a timer (cron). Triggered = fires when an external webhook hits the recipe's URL.
type.example: Daily reports → Scheduled | CI/CD → Triggered | Ad-hoc → Manual

cron_expression.text: A 5-field cron expression that defines when the recipe runs. Format: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. Use the quick picks for common schedules or write your own.
cron_expression.example: 0 9 * * 1-5 = weekdays at 9am | 0 */4 * * * = every 4 hours | 30 23 * * * = daily at 11:30pm

webhook.text: A unique URL that triggers this recipe when it receives a POST request. The JSON body is passed as input data to the first step. Use this to integrate with GitHub webhooks, Jira, Slack, etc.

mode.text: Sequential runs steps one after another — each step can use the previous step's output. Parallel runs all steps at once — faster but steps must be independent (no shared data between them).

max_retries.text: How many times to retry a failed step before giving up. 0 = no retries, fail immediately. Higher values add resilience against transient LLM errors or rate limits.

step_timeout.text: Maximum time (in milliseconds) a single step can run before being killed. Prevents runaway agents. 60000ms = 1 minute. Complex tasks may need 5-10 minutes.

total_timeout.text: Maximum time for the entire recipe execution. If this limit is reached, all remaining steps are cancelled. Should be greater than step_timeout × number_of_steps.

auto_learning.text: When enabled, the platform analyses each execution to find patterns — which steps fail, which are slow, which produce the best results. Uses this data to suggest optimisations.

parallel_limit.text: Maximum number of steps that can run simultaneously in parallel mode. Lower = less resource contention. Higher = faster execution. Only applies when execution mode is Parallel.

memory_isolation.text: Shared = all steps access the same conversation memory (step 2 sees step 1's output). Isolated = each step starts fresh with no knowledge of other steps. Use shared for pipelines, isolated for independent tasks.

time_range.text: Filter by date range. Options: 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days, or custom.

search.text: Search by name, description, or tags. Case-insensitive, updates in real-time.

refresh.text: Reload data from the server. Use if data seems stale.

export.text: Export data as CSV for external analysis or reporting.
